courseTitle: Web Development with Antigravity AI Agent

modules.title: Start Your Web Development Journey with Google Antigravity AI Agent!
objectives: Set up a web development project in Google Antigravity.
Use the Antigravity Agent to generate and edit code with natural language prompts.
Create a basic web page using HTML.
Apply styles to page elements using CSS.
Create light and dark themes using CSS.
Add support for switching between themes using JavaScript.
Review Artifacts generated by the Antigravity Agent.

units.title: Introduction
units.content:
## Introduction

It's impressive what you can do on the web today. You can build web experiences that run on all devices, include all sorts of media content, and perform complicated computation. You can even create apps that look and feel like native applications.

If you're interested in starting web development today, you might be faced with a dizzying array of options. In this module, you'll learn the basic components of a website and how to use **Google Antigravity** — an agentic development platform — to accelerate your web development workflow. You'll use HTML, CSS, and JavaScript together to build a website, and you'll direct the Antigravity Agent using natural language prompts to do much of the heavy lifting.

With this fundamental knowledge in place, you'll have a better context to make decisions in the future when building websites — for example, whether you should choose JavaScript frameworks or create your own JavaScript functions to build your website.

### Scenario

Imagine that you're a web developer, and you've been asked to make your company's website appeal to a broader range of customers. To allow your customers to customize their experience on your website, you decide to add support for **light and dark themes**. You create a small, proof-of-concept website to demonstrate support for themes using CSS, and you write a JavaScript function to toggle between these themes.

When completed, your website will have:
- A structured HTML page with a task list
- A CSS file defining both a light and a dark theme
- A JavaScript file that toggles between themes on button click

### What's in a web page?

The content, style, and interactive logic of a web page are separated into three distinct file types:

| File Type | Role | Example |
|-----------|------|---------|
| **HTML** | Structure and content | Headings, paragraphs, lists, buttons |
| **CSS** | Visual presentation | Colors, fonts, layout, spacing |
| **JavaScript** | Interactivity and behavior | Button clicks, animations, data fetching |

A key design principle in modern programming is **separation of concerns**. By keeping these three layers separate, you make your code simpler to maintain and easier to reuse. For example, a single CSS file can style dozens of HTML pages consistently, without repeating style rules in every file.

### Why Google Antigravity?

Google Antigravity is an **agent-first development platform**. Rather than writing every line of code manually, you describe what you want to build in plain language, and the Antigravity Agent generates, reviews, and executes the code for you. This lets you focus on the *what* and the *why* — not just the *how*.

Key features you'll use in this course:
- **Agent**: Responds to natural language prompts to write and modify code
- **Artifacts**: Visual summaries of what the agent plans to do (Implementation Plans, Walkthroughs)
- **Tab**: Intelligent autocomplete within the editor
- **Projects**: Organized workspaces that give the agent the right context
units.actionAssignment: Before moving on, think about a website you visit frequently. Can you identify which parts of the page might be structured with HTML, styled with CSS, and made interactive with JavaScript?

units.title: Exercise — Set up your environment
units.content:
## Exercise — Set up your environment

In this exercise, you'll install Google Antigravity and create your first web development project. Antigravity uses a **project-centric approach** to ensure its AI agents have access to the right files, tools, and permissions.

### Step 1: Install Google Antigravity

If you haven't already, download and install Google Antigravity from the [official website](https://antigravity.google/download). The installer is available for macOS, Linux, and Windows.

1. Go to **antigravity.google/download** and download the installer for your operating system.
2. Run the installer and follow the on-screen instructions.
3. Sign in with your **Google account** when prompted.
4. Accept the Security and Data Use policy, then click **Next**.
5. Select a theme you like (you can change this later), then click **Finish**.

You should now see the Antigravity interface — a clean, chat-based workspace with a project panel on the left.

> **Tip:** You can optionally also install the **Antigravity IDE** from the same download page. The IDE provides a full VS Code-style editing experience with the agent panel built in. For this course, either the standalone Antigravity app or the IDE will work.

---

### Step 2: Create your project folder using the Terminal

Before creating a project in Antigravity, you need to create a folder on your computer to hold your web project files. The fastest and most reliable way to do this is with your operating system's **terminal** (also called the command line or shell).

The terminal is a text-based interface that lets you control your computer by typing commands. Developers use it constantly — it's faster than clicking through folders, and it's how you'll interact with many tools throughout your career.

#### How to open the terminal on your operating system

:::terminal-demo:::

#### Run the command to create your folder

Once your terminal is open, type the following command and press **Enter**:

:::mkdir-demo:::

After running the command, verify the folder was created by listing the contents of your home directory:

:::verify-demo:::

> **What just happened?** The `mkdir` command (**m**a**k**e **dir**ectory) created a new empty folder at the path you specified. The `~` symbol is a shortcut for your home directory (e.g., `/Users/yourname` on Mac, `/home/yourname` on Linux, or `C:\Users\yourname` on Windows).

---

### Step 3: Create a project in Antigravity

1. In the Antigravity interface, click **Select Project** → **New Project**.
2. Click **Add Folder** and navigate to select the `my-web-project` folder you just created.
3. Click **Next**.
4. Choose the **Default** security preset. This means the agent will ask for your review before executing terminal commands.
5. Give your project a name — for example, `my-web-project` — and click **Create**.

Your project is now set up! You should see it listed in the left navigation bar, and the chat interface is ready for your first prompt.

### Understanding Projects

A **project** in Antigravity is a combination of one or more folders that define the scope of your agent's work. The agent can only read and write files within the folders you've added to the project. Each project has its own isolated security settings, so you can control exactly what the agent is allowed to do.

| Setting | Description |
|---------|-------------|
| **Security Preset** | Controls whether terminal commands require your review |
| **Agent Behaviour** | Controls whether the agent executes plans automatically or waits for approval |
| **File Permissions** | Specific file paths the agent is allowed or blocked from accessing |
| **MCP Tools** | Which external tool integrations are available to the agent |
units.actionAssignment: Verify your project is set up correctly by greeting the Antigravity Agent in the chat interface. Type 'Hello! I'm going to build a web page today.' and see how it responds.

units.content:
## Module assessment

Test your understanding of the concepts covered in this module. Answer all questions correctly to earn your completion badge.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the primary purpose of an HTML file in a web project?
options: To define the visual styles and colors of the page
To define the structure and content of the web page
To add interactivity and respond to user events
To configure the web server settings
knowledgeCheck.explanation: HTML (HyperText Markup Language) defines the structure and content of a web page — headings, paragraphs, lists, buttons, and so on. CSS handles visual styles, and JavaScript handles interactivity.

knowledgeCheck.question: In Google Antigravity, what is an 'Artifact'?
options: A bug or error found in your code
A configuration file for the agent
Something the agent creates to communicate its work or plan — such as an Implementation Plan, Walkthrough, or code diff
A backup copy of your project files
knowledgeCheck.explanation: Artifacts are rich outputs that the Antigravity Agent produces to communicate its plans and accomplishments. They include Implementation Plans (before writing code), Walkthroughs (after completing a task), code diffs, screenshots, and more.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which CSS technique is used to implement a dark theme in this module?
options: A separate HTML file for the dark version of the page
Inline styles applied directly to each element
A CSS class (e.g., .dark-theme) applied to the <body> element
A CSS media query for prefers-color-scheme
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The dark theme is implemented by defining a .dark-theme CSS class with overriding styles, and then toggling that class on the <body> element using JavaScript's classList.toggle() method.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does classList.toggle('dark-theme') do in JavaScript?
options: It always adds the 'dark-theme' class to the element
It always removes the 'dark-theme' class from the element
It adds the class if it's absent, or removes it if it's already present
It checks whether the element has the class and returns true or false
knowledgeCheck.explanation: classList.toggle() is a convenient method that adds a class if the element doesn't have it, or removes it if the element already has it — perfect for implementing a toggle button.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the purpose of the 'Implementation Plan' artifact in Antigravity?
options: It is a log of all the files the agent has previously modified
It is a plan the agent shows you before writing code, so you can review and approve its intended actions
It is a deployment checklist for publishing your website
It is a summary of errors found in your code
knowledgeCheck.explanation: The Implementation Plan is an artifact the Antigravity Agent generates before making any changes. It describes what the agent intends to do, allowing you to review and either approve or redirect the plan before any code is written.

units.title: Summary
units.content:
## Summary

Congratulations on completing this module! You've taken your first steps into web development using Google Antigravity.

### What you accomplished

In this module, you built a complete, interactive web page from scratch. Here's a recap of what you created:

| File | What it does |
|------|-------------|
| `index.html` | The structure of your Task List page |
| `style.css` | The visual styles, including both light and dark themes |
| `app.js` | The interactivity — populating tasks and toggling the theme |

### Skills you practiced

- **Setting up a project** in Google Antigravity using the project-centric workspace model.
- **Prompting the Antigravity Agent** with clear, structured natural language to generate code.
- **Reviewing Artifacts** — Implementation Plans and Walkthroughs — to understand and verify the agent's work before and after execution.
- **HTML fundamentals**: boilerplate structure, semantic elements, linking CSS and JS files.
- **CSS fundamentals**: selectors, properties, the cascade, and class-based theming.
- **JavaScript fundamentals**: DOM selection, event listeners, classList manipulation, and dynamic element creation.

### The agent-first advantage

By using Google Antigravity, you were able to focus on *what* you wanted to build rather than memorizing every syntax detail. The agent handled the boilerplate, the file linking, and the implementation details — while you stayed in control by reviewing every plan before it executed.

This is the promise of agent-first development: **you bring the ideas, the agent brings the implementation speed.**

### What's next?

Now that you understand the fundamentals, consider exploring:

- **CSS Flexbox and Grid** for more complex layouts
- **JavaScript fetch()** for loading data from APIs
- **Antigravity's Browser Agent** for automated UI testing of your web pages
- **MCP Server integrations** in Antigravity for connecting your projects to external services

### Final reflection

Think about how using Antigravity changed your development workflow compared to writing every line of code manually. How might this agent-first approach change the way you plan and execute future software projects?

modules.title: Build a dynamic web app with Antigravity and a REST API
objectives: Understand what a REST API is and how the web uses HTTP to exchange data.
Use the Antigravity Agent to fetch data from a public REST API.
Parse and display JSON data dynamically in the browser.
Handle loading states and errors gracefully in your UI.
Use async/await and the Fetch API to write clean asynchronous JavaScript.
Extend your existing web project with new features using Antigravity.

units.title: Introduction
units.content:
## Introduction

In Module 1, you built a static task list web page with light and dark theme support. The tasks were hardcoded directly in your JavaScript file. In the real world, web applications fetch their data dynamically from **servers** — and they do this using **REST APIs**.

In this module, you'll extend your web project to fetch live data from a public REST API, display it on the page, and handle the asynchronous nature of network requests. As before, you'll use the **Antigravity Agent** to help you write and refine the code.

### Scenario

Your company's task list app has been a hit internally. Now the team wants to load tasks from a real backend server instead of hardcoding them. You'll use the free [JSONPlaceholder API](https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/) — a public fake REST API for testing — to simulate fetching tasks from a server.

When completed, your app will:
- Fetch a list of todos from `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos`
- Display them dynamically on the page with their completion status
- Show a loading spinner while the request is in flight
- Show a user-friendly error message if the request fails

### What is a REST API?

A **REST API** (Representational State Transfer Application Programming Interface) is a standardized way for software systems to communicate over the web. When your browser visits a URL, it sends an **HTTP request** to a server. The server responds with data — often formatted as **JSON** (JavaScript Object Notation).

| HTTP Method | Purpose | Example |
|------------|---------|---------|
| `GET` | Retrieve data | Fetch a list of todos |
| `POST` | Create new data | Add a new todo |
| `PUT` | Update existing data | Mark a todo as complete |
| `DELETE` | Remove data | Delete a todo |

In this module, you'll focus on the `GET` method — reading data from the API.

### What is JSON?

JSON is the most common data format used by REST APIs. It looks like a JavaScript object:

```json
{
  "id": 1,
  "title": "Buy groceries",
  "completed": false,
  "userId": 1
}
```

JavaScript can parse JSON natively using `JSON.parse()`, and the modern `fetch()` API can do this automatically with `.json()`.

### The Antigravity advantage for async code

Asynchronous programming — writing code that waits for network requests without freezing the browser — is one of the trickier aspects of JavaScript. The Antigravity Agent excels here: you can describe the behavior you want in plain language, and it will generate correct `async/await` patterns, error handling, and loading state logic for you.
units.actionAssignment: Open your browser and navigate to https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos?_limit=5. You should see a JSON array of 5 todo objects. This is the data your app will fetch and display.

units.title: Exercise — Handle loading states and errors
units.content:
## Exercise — Handle loading states and errors

A production-quality web app must handle the real world gracefully: slow connections, server outages, and unexpected data. In this exercise, you'll improve the robustness of your app.

### Why error handling matters

Without error handling, a failed network request leaves your user staring at a spinning loader forever. Good error handling means:
- The user always knows what's happening
- The app recovers gracefully from failures
- Developers get useful diagnostic information

### Step 1: Add a retry button

Prompt the Antigravity Agent:

```
Update the error handling in app.js and index.html:
1. Add a <button id="retry-btn"> inside the #error-message div with the text "Try again".
2. In app.js, extract the fetch logic into a separate async function called loadTasks().
3. Call loadTasks() on DOMContentLoaded.
4. Add a click event listener to #retry-btn that clears the task list, hides the error, and calls loadTasks() again.
```

### Step 2: Add a timeout

Network requests can hang indefinitely. Prompt the Agent to add a timeout:

```
Add a 5-second timeout to the fetch call in loadTasks(). If the request takes longer than 5 seconds, abort it and show the error message with the text "Request timed out. Please check your connection."
Use AbortController for the timeout.
```

### Understanding AbortController

```javascript
const controller = new AbortController();
const timeoutId = setTimeout(() => controller.abort(), 5000);

try {
  const response = await fetch(url, { signal: controller.signal });
  clearTimeout(timeoutId);
  // ... process response
} catch (error) {
  if (error.name === 'AbortError') {
    throw new Error('Request timed out. Please check your connection.');
  }
  throw error;
}
```

### Step 3: Add a loading skeleton

Instead of plain text, show placeholder skeleton items while loading. Prompt the Agent:

```
Update style.css to add a .skeleton class: a gray rounded rectangle (height 1.2rem, background #e0e0e0) with a CSS animation that pulses the opacity from 0.4 to 1 and back, repeating infinitely over 1.5 seconds.

Update app.js to show 5 skeleton <li> elements with the .skeleton class while loading, then replace them with real data when it arrives.
```

### Error states reference

| Error type | Cause | User message |
|-----------|-------|-------------|
| `TypeError: Failed to fetch` | No internet connection | "No internet connection. Please check your network." |
| `AbortError` | Request timed out | "Request timed out. Please try again." |
| HTTP 404 | Resource not found | "The requested data could not be found." |
| HTTP 500 | Server error | "The server encountered an error. Please try again later." |
units.actionAssignment: Test your retry button by temporarily changing the API URL to an invalid one (e.g., add 'xxx' to the end). Does the error message appear? Does clicking 'Try again' work after fixing the URL?

units.title: Exercise — Send data with POST requests
units.content:
## Exercise — Send data with POST requests

So far you've only read data from the API. Now you'll learn to **send** data — adding a new todo via a `POST` request.

### What is a POST request?

A `POST` request sends data to the server to create a new resource. Unlike `GET`, it includes a **request body** containing the data to be created, typically formatted as JSON.

```javascript
const response = await fetch('https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: {
    'Content-Type': 'application/json',
  },
  body: JSON.stringify({
    title: 'My new task',
    completed: false,
    userId: 1,
  }),
});
const newTodo = await response.json();
console.log(newTodo); // { id: 201, title: 'My new task', ... }
```

> **Note:** JSONPlaceholder is a fake API — it simulates creating a resource and returns a response with a new `id`, but nothing is actually saved to a real database.

### Step 1: Add a form to your HTML

Prompt the Antigravity Agent:

```
Add a form to index.html above the task list:
- A <form id="add-task-form"> with:
  - A text <input id="new-task-input" placeholder="Add a new task...">
  - A <button type="submit"> with the text "Add Task"
- Style the form so the input and button are on the same line (use flexbox).
- Add the form styles to style.css, consistent with the existing design.
```

### Step 2: Handle form submission with a POST request

```
In app.js, add an event listener for the #add-task-form submit event:
1. Prevent the default form submission with event.preventDefault().
2. Read the value from #new-task-input. If empty, do nothing.
3. Disable the submit button and change its text to "Adding..." while the request is in progress.
4. Send a POST request to https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/todos with:
   - method: 'POST'
   - Content-Type: application/json header
   - body: JSON.stringify({ title: inputValue, completed: false, userId: 1 })
5. On success, add the new todo as a <li> at the TOP of the task list (prepend, not append).
6. Clear the input field and re-enable the submit button.
7. On error, show an alert with the error message.
```

### Understanding the fetch options object

| Option | Type | Purpose |
|--------|------|---------|
| `method` | string | HTTP method: `'GET'`, `'POST'`, `'PUT'`, `'DELETE'` |
| `headers` | object | HTTP headers — `Content-Type` tells the server the body format |
| `body` | string | The request body — must be a string, so use `JSON.stringify()` |
| `signal` | AbortSignal | For cancelling the request (from AbortController) |

### Step 3: Optimistic UI update

Prompt the Agent to improve the UX:

```
Modify the form submission handler to use an "optimistic update" pattern:
1. Immediately add the new task to the top of the list (before the API call completes), with a slightly faded appearance (opacity: 0.6) and the text "(saving...)".
2. When the POST request succeeds, update the list item to full opacity and remove "(saving...)".
3. If the POST request fails, remove the optimistically added item and show the error.
```

This pattern makes the app feel instant to the user, even over slow connections.
units.actionAssignment: Type a new task in the form and click 'Add Task'. Does the task appear at the top of the list? Open the browser's Network tab (DevTools → Network) and find the POST request — what status code did the server return?

units.title: Module assessment
units.content:
## Module assessment

Test your understanding of REST APIs, the Fetch API, and asynchronous JavaScript. Answer all questions correctly to earn your completion badge.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does the `await` keyword do inside an `async` function?
options: It runs the code in a separate background thread
It pauses execution of the async function until the Promise resolves, without blocking the browser
It converts a callback-based function into a Promise
It makes the function run synchronously
knowledgeCheck.explanation: `await` pauses the execution of the surrounding `async` function until the awaited Promise settles. Crucially, it does NOT block the browser's main thread — other code and UI interactions can still run while waiting.

knowledgeCheck.question: Which HTTP method should you use to retrieve a list of todos from a REST API?
options: POST
PUT
DELETE
GET
knowledgeCheck.explanation: GET is the correct HTTP method for retrieving data. POST creates new resources, PUT updates existing ones, and DELETE removes them. REST APIs follow this convention consistently.

knowledgeCheck.question: What does `response.ok` check in a fetch response?
options: Whether the response body is valid JSON
Whether the network request completed without timing out
Whether the HTTP status code is in the 200–299 range (success)
Whether the server returned any data at all
knowledgeCheck.explanation: `response.ok` is `true` when the HTTP status code is between 200 and 299, indicating a successful response. It is `false` for 4xx (client errors) and 5xx (server errors) status codes. Note that `fetch()` itself only rejects on network failures — you must check `response.ok` manually for HTTP errors.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is the purpose of `JSON.stringify()` when sending a POST request?
options: To compress the data for faster transmission
To convert a JavaScript object into a JSON string, which is required for the request body
To validate that the data matches the API schema
To encrypt the data before sending it to the server
knowledgeCheck.explanation: HTTP request bodies must be strings (or binary data). `JSON.stringify()` converts a JavaScript object into its JSON string representation so it can be sent in the request body. The `Content-Type: application/json` header tells the server how to interpret that string.

knowledgeCheck.question: What is an 'optimistic UI update'?
options: Showing the user a success message before the API call is made, without any rollback on failure
Immediately updating the UI as if the operation succeeded, then correcting it if the server returns an error
Caching API responses to avoid making network requests
Disabling the UI while an API request is in progress
knowledgeCheck.explanation: An optimistic update immediately reflects the expected outcome in the UI before the server confirms it, making the app feel instant. If the server returns an error, the UI is rolled back to its previous state. This pattern is common in modern apps like Twitter/X (liking a tweet) and Gmail (sending an email).

units.title: Summary
units.content:
## Summary

Congratulations on completing Module 2! You've taken a significant step forward — from a static web page to a dynamic web application that communicates with a real server.

### What you built

| Feature | Technology |
|---------|-----------|
| Fetch todos from a server | `fetch()` API + JSONPlaceholder |
| Handle loading states | DOM manipulation + CSS skeleton animation |
| Handle network errors | `try/catch` + AbortController timeout |
| Retry failed requests | Extracted `loadTasks()` function |
| Add new todos via form | `POST` request + `JSON.stringify()` |
| Optimistic UI updates | Immediate DOM update + rollback on error |

### Skills you practiced

- **REST API fundamentals**: HTTP methods, status codes, JSON data format
- **Fetch API**: `async/await`, `response.ok`, `response.json()`, request options
- **Error handling**: `try/catch`, AbortController, user-friendly error messages
- **Antigravity Agent**: Using natural language to generate async JavaScript patterns, refactor code, and add features incrementally

### The agent-first advantage, revisited

Asynchronous JavaScript is notoriously tricky to get right — especially error handling, race conditions, and loading states. By describing the behavior you wanted in plain language, the Antigravity Agent generated correct, production-quality patterns that would have taken much longer to write manually.

### What's next?

You now have the foundation to build real-world web applications. Consider exploring:

- **Authentication**: Adding a login flow to your app using OAuth or JWT tokens
- **A real backend**: Building your own REST API with Node.js and Express, using Antigravity to scaffold it
- **Frameworks**: Exploring React or Vue.js for more complex UIs — and using Antigravity's multi-file awareness to manage larger codebases
- **Deployment**: Using Antigravity's Browser Agent to automate deployment to a cloud platform
units.actionAssignment: Your app now fetches and displays real data from the internet. Share it with a colleague and ask them to add a task. What would you need to change to make the added tasks actually persist after a page refresh?
